subtopic: STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week when we were discussing the unemployment figures for the month of April I promised to make a statement on motions pertaining to the possibility of extending seasonal benefits. First, in discussing this matter, I think I should emphasize that seasonal benefits
are available under the Unemployment Insurance Act for the period between December 1 and May 15 and are payable to those who have a very minimal attachment to the labour force but are unable to qualify for regular benefits. Eligibility is based on much less rigid qualifying conditions but is not limited to those who work in seasonal occupations. In this context it must be emphasized that the basic purpose of unemployment insurance is to provide benefits for relatively short-term periods of unemployment. Under both the present program and the new program, a maximum duration of 51 or 52 weeks is considered the right period of time, with an average duration per claim of about 14 weeks.
The case for extending seasonal benefits could possibly rest on two points: First, the relatively higher unemployment rate for this time of year and hence the relatively greater difficulty of finding work; second, the assumption that people whose benefits terminate at the end of the seasonal benefit period will automatically begin drawing welfare. By this reasoning, the assumption is made that the 200,000 claimants whose benefits terminated on May 15 require a continuation of financial assistance and that the simplest method of assistance would be to extend the benefits for further periods of time.
With regard to the case against extension, while the extension of seasonal benefits appears to be a relatively automatic and simple type of adjustment, I would like to explain the reasons why it did not appear to the government that we should take this measure at this time.
Although the level of unemployment for this time of year is higher than in past years and higher than had been anticipated for the month of April, I would like to emphasize that the number of people drawing seasonal benefits is not correspondingly higher this year than the number who were drawing seasonal benefits in former years at this particular time of the year. I might add that the number of people drawing seasonal benefits on May 15 last year was 180,000 as opposed to 200,000 this year and 160,000 in 1969.
Of these estimated 200,000 claimants who were drawing seasonal benefits at the end of April, there would be approximately 40,000 in the fishing industry and 12,000 in agriculture. These industries can be identified separately because of the distinct contribution system for them, but in addition it is known that there are many tens of thousands of people in forestry, water transportation and other industries whose period of unemployment could reasonably be expected to end at this time.
Studies carried out by the commission of the recipients of seasonal benefits have indicated that more than 60 per cent of such claimants are back at work at or about the

May 19, 1971
Unemployment Insurance
time that seasonal benefits terminate. These studies have also shown that there is another large group of claimants who have, for all intents and purposes, left the labour force voluntarily and in some cases have been on prolonged claims for periods of up to 70 weeks. Included in this group would be those who have left the labour force because of age, retirement or occupations in the home.
It has also been observed in the studies mentioned earlier that seasonal benefits in certain occupations and regions have come to influence the pattern of work where recalls by employers and the return to work by employees are made to coincide with the end of the seasonal benefits period.
There is no evidence that persons exhausting seasonal benefits necessarily go on welfare. We have analysed figures over a number of years of the numbers of unemployed employables on welfare in certain cities and there is no significant indication that welfare rolls increase significantly as a result of the termination of seasonal benefits, or conversely that welfare rolls decline on December 1 with the start of seasonal benefits. Indeed, it is generally accepted that the increase in welfare beneficiaries during the past few years has come mainly from that part of the population not now covered by unemployment insurance or unable to qualify under the present rules.
All these considerations point to the fact that the extension of seasonal benefits would have the tendency of providing an automatic benefit to a substantial number of people who may in fact no longer be members of the labour force. On the other hand, it would not in any way change the situation for those who cannot qualify for unemployment insurance benefits under the present rules.
To conclude, the cost of extending benefits even for a period of let us say six weeks ending June 27 would be between $35 million and $45 million. The government believes that because of the difficulty of clearly determining those among recipients of seasonal benefits who would deserve assistance, this would not be the best way of spending such a large sum of money.
The white paper on unemployment insurance and Bill C-229 both propose that the solution to the problem of people who do not qualify for regular benefits rests primarily on lower eligibility conditions and a method of extension of benefits which reflects the economic conditions at national and regional levels. We feel so strongly about these features that we are proposing to abolish the present method of paying seasonal benefits. This has been endorsed almost unanimously by all those who have expressed views on the white paper and on Bill C-229. Because these will be in effect very soon, I believe that the extension of seasonal benefits at this stage under the circumstances I have just explained would not be desirable at this time.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) quite properly asked for some added information in the form of a breakdown of the characteristics of the 348,000 Canadians reported out of work for more than four months as of mid-April. It is a detailed answer, Mr. Speaker. I have

sent a copy of it on to the hon. gentleman, but based upon the findings that we have been able to come up with it would appear that approximately 300,000 of these
348,000	people who have been unemployed for 14 weeks or more are drawing or were drawing unemployment insurance at the time the latest statistics became available.

I listened to the minister in utter disbelief. It appears to me that his role is to be the nice guy. His role as minister is to palliate, while the role of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is to throw red herrings into important discussions similar to this one. When thousands have been unemployed for so long that they have lost all their benefits, and the cities are being crippled by welfare payments, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) will not bring in any extension of benefits for seasonal workers, which in effect would reduce the tension and lack of confidence that are permeating our entire society.
With six weeks to go to the target date for implementation of the new Unemployment Insurance Act the minister has suddenly been gripped by the urgency of the plight of the unemployed. But apparently his only concern about them is to attempt to mitigate or explain away their situation. He has not given us a statement of purpose, a statement that would indicate to the unemployed that something is going to be done. Rather, he has given a statement indicating that he is going to bring in some relief to alleviate the situation on July 1.
The minister and the government have become so smug and snug that they have lost touch with the frustrations and despair that go along with being out of work for any length of time or with being out of work-period. The Minister of Labour leaves the impression that he is above it all. The minister wants the country to believe that he is the conscience of the Liberal party, of Pearson, King and St. Laurent, and that his job is to be the humane flank for an inhumane government. I suppose that is why he had the audacity to make this statement today, or maybe he would like to leave the impression that he does not know what is going on in the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a smug statement from a minister reflecting the thinking of a smug cabinet which has lost completely its touch and its concern for the average person in this country. The average person in this country, whether he happens to be working or not and many are not right now, is concerned about the very high level of unemployment that exists, because all of us are affected directly or indirectly.
Given the pious expressions which have come from this minister in the past one would have hoped that he would find reasons and a method to extend the seasonal benefits. He did not come before us today as he did the other day and suggest that there was no possibility of extending benefits within the present legislation because apparently he found that there is that legal possibility and he could have acted had he so desired. Instead, he presented to us a loosely connected batch of arguments that do not hold water.
First of all, he suggested that the number of people drawing seasonal benefits is no higher than at this time of the year in the past. Second, he said that a number of farmers, fishermen and others who are seasonally unemployed would be going back to work soon. I should like to remind the minister that one of his obligations is to check statistics rather carefully. If he does he will find that, compared with this time last year, there is now an increase of 30 per cent in the numbers of those drawing seasonal benefits. The figure has gone from 172,000 to some 223,000 which is, I repeat, a 30 per cent increase. It is not a constant figure.

Furthermore, when the minister says that a number of those people will soon be going back to work, I suggest that he look at the speeches made recently in this House, one yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and one last week by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang). In those speeches those ministers pointed out that because of the exceptional winter we have faced, because of the prolonged cold and so on we are perhaps at least one month behind in catching up with the normal seasonal increase in the numbers of employed. That, it seems to me, provides within the context of government arguments good reason for extending seasonal benefits. Two responsible ministers in the cabinet have said that this country is lagging behind as a result in part of a severe winter. That is what seasonal benefits are all about. If there is a lag, why then does the government not extend seasonal benefits?
The third argument that the minister trotted out for us to consider is that normally those who go off seasonal benefits do not go on the welfare roles. He referred to a study which shows this. I suggest that the government is under the minimum obligation of tabling in the House that study which documents that purported fact. It may be the case that in the past a number of those who went off seasonal benefits did not go on welfare. That may have been true when only 130,000 people were involved. Nevertheless, if 200,000 people are now getting such benefits and are cut off, I suggest to the government that it is an elementary step of logic to expect that a very large percentage of them will find themselves on the welfare rolls across the country. So much for the third argument, Mr. Speaker. I use the word "argument" in a flattering sense, because I do not think what the minister actually presented amounted to arguments.
This government has produced the highest level of unemployment in this country in a decade and is now obligated to do something about it. We heard the Minister of Finance yesterday say effectively that he will not change his course of action. I, for one, had hoped that the Minister of Labour, who of all men ought to be concerned about the average people in this country, would come before the House, acknowledge the facts about the seasonal situation we have gone through in the past winter, a situation that was acknowledged by two other cabinet ministers, and extend seasonal benefits. But no, he has not done that. He has joined the Minister of Finance and his other smug colleagues and is sitting this very serious problem out on the front benches of the government. I suggest that if the minister is concerned about the average person in this country, he ought to follow the two hon. members who were recently cabinet ministers and become a backbencher in the Liberal party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I would like to seek unanimous consent of the House to move a motion. My motion arises out of a continuing series of statements by the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission to the effect that inflation remains Canada's number one economic enemy in spite of clear evidence that anti-inflationary policies have contributed to the present unemployment crisis. Because Dr. Young's statements are doing great harm to economic recovery, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the present chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission be dismissed forthwith and that, if the commission is to be retained as a government agency, its functions be redefined to prevent its chairman from being a propagandist and apologist for disastrous policies.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-ASSISTANCE FOR THOSE WITHOUT INSURANCE BENEFITS-AID TO PROVINCES AND MUNICIPALITIES TO MEET WELFARE COSTS

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak on the motion and the amendment before us this afternoon, I feel that the discussion which might follow this afternoon and on other days might be effectively shortened if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) would indicate in more clear and precise terms than he did last Thursday what in fact the government is willing to accept by way of terms of reference for this joint parliamentary committee which is to be established. If indeed the Minister of Justice, speaking on behalf of his colleagues, can indicate that the government is prepared to accept the reasonable amendment put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), then I think that we could very effectively and efficiently move on to discuss other business in the House. I would be quite willing to yield the floor at this point to the Minister of Justice if he would indicate an acceptance of the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: I will wait until you end your speech.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
The minister says he will wait until the end of my speech. That is very charitable of him. He expects that I have something worthwhile to add to the debate and I appreciate that. Quite frankly, one of the difficulties we are faced with this afternoon, and one of the difficulties that created the amendment proposed last Thursday, is the fact that we are asked to accept a task, to answer certain basic questions, without having clearly defined for us the nature of the problem.
If the events of the October crisis can only be responded to at this distance in time, some half a year later, by the suggestion that we need new kinds of legislation to deal with lawlessness and violence, surely that proposal coming from the government represents a poverty of thought. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it indicates the degree to which the government has now become very unsure of the wisdom of the position it took last fall, and is unwilling at this point to go any further than to say let us have a parliamentary committee to bring in some kind of law that is not quite as nasty as the War Measures Act.
We were told as recently as last Sunday evening by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that, while the government does not want to suggest to the committee what it would like to see in terms of proposed legislation, the Prime Minister did suggest on this same television program that there were gaps in the law which must be filled. He said, in effect, "We have various alternatives for filling these gaps but we want Members of Parliament and the country at large to discuss this thing very freely." What does the Prime Minister mean by that? Is this to be a parliamentary game of blindman's buff in which the members of the committee try and discern what it is the government really has in mind, or are we invited to participate in some kind of shadow boxing exercise over one of the gravest events that has occurred in this country in recent times? Surely, neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Justice can be that childish about an event of such major significance that they would play this kind of game with Members of Parliament and with the public.
Indeed, the position of members of this chamber may be worse than that, Mr. Speaker, because, along with the proposal for establishing this committee, it is suggested by the government that if the committee does not do its job properly or if a crisis occurs such as the one last fall

we have never really been told exactly what that means though we have been given various renditions of what it means-the government will not shrink from responding in a similar fashion. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on last Sunday's program "Weekend", said:
-if a new crisis like the October one breaks out, then we will introduce special laws very quickly-
We have not told what they might be, whether they will be a return to the public order bill or some other legislation. He continued:
-and if the violence is of such a nature that special laws are bogged down in such a way that we cannot meet the crisis, we will resort again to the War Measures Act. There's

May 19, 1971

no ambiguity on that, and if people don't feel protected, let me just tell them that we will do as well in the future as we did in October-
One can almost imagine some of the Hallelujah choruses coming out of the background at that point. What we have here is some form of parliamentary blackmail. If the members of this chamber do not get on with the job, then the government implies they have the muscle, they have the tools to do the job and are prepared to go to bat again as they did last fall.
For those who are concerned about the present situation, as is the Premier of Quebec, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) have tried to offer comfort by saying, "Of course, we still have the Criminal Code and we can still act under such sections as seditious conspiracy; we can certainly deal with people who would have the aims and approaches of those active in the FLQ." I really admire the intestinal fortitude of anybody who can make that statement now, in the month of May, when last October they were telling us how important it was to have other repressive laws to do the job. That kind of double thinking, however, does not seem to bother the members of this government to any degree.
In all the discussions that have surrounded the events of last October, both in this chamber and in the country, one of the real problems has been how to get at the basic issues. I suppose it is always the case that when a country's emotions are engaged, when it is faced with an event that its leaders describe as an insurrection and a crisis and when there is talk of revolutionary activity, then the people are inclined to respond to the most emotional aspects of the events. But surely one of the benefits of looking back with sober second thoughts at the events of last fall is that we can go to the heart of the basic issues, that we can ask basic questions, that we do not have to be mislead by requests for laws to cover events that we cannot look at. How can we frame laws in such a way that they will be appropriate for future situations which nobody has described? If the government feels itself caught in that trap, I believe that there are many reasonable and intelligent people in the country and in this Parliament who do not feel caught.
There are three main issues, Mr. Speaker, which I contend must be looked at soberly and rationally. I want to speak about these this afternoon because they should form the background for any committee activity if that committee is going to be responsible in the face of a crisis such as that of last fall and the actions of the government last fall.
The first is the issue of violence. For most people, this is where the discussion usually starts and ends because violence is such an irrational act, because violence is so unpredictable and because it so often dramatic and final. It has a kind of magnetic quality. It is no wonder that the written, visual and oral press give so much attention to violence. We sometimes accuse the press of paying too much attention to it, but I think any thoughtful pressman would reply that they pay attention to violence because people are fascinated by it. I do not know whether it is true to suggest, as many people have, that we live in a
National Security Measures
violent age-maybe it is just reported more extensively and effectively.
There is no doubt that our society, like most, is troubled by violence from time to time. In its preoccupation and concern with the violence of last October, the government has suggested that there are gaps in the law, that we really do not have the proper instruments in law to deal with violence, that when there is lawlessness and a government is endangered through violence we do not seem to have the appropriate means to combat it. Surely, the government has fallen into the classic trap of immediately jumping to consequences before examining the causes, Mr. Speaker. It might be suggested at this point, I suppose, that if someone is running down the street firing a machine gun one does not resort to a study to determine the cause of such irrational behaviour. Of course, this is true but if some violent event has occurred in the past in a variety of ways, and one has tried to deal with it on the short term, surely there then comes a time when it must be dealt with on the long term. Surely, if we now have this moment to reflect without the pressure of immediate events of a violent nature, one of the first questions to ask is what the roots of violence are and what the causes of violence are.
It has often been suggested in this chamber that the causes of violence in our society today are social and economic inequality. Last fall a number of people suggested that the very serious economic situation in the province of Quebec could well have formed the social fabric out of which arose the acts of violence associated with the FLQ. Last Sunday evening the Prime Minister suggested that there are other parts of the country where there has been exceptionally high unemployment. He referred to the Maritimes, the area that I know best, and he said that there has not been the same kind of violence there. There is some measure of truth in this, but only some because often the very fact of high unemployment merely represents a deeper malaise. I do not think it takes a very acute observer to realize that there have been some long term problems and social discontent in the province of Quebec. Those who have read some of the current literature emanating from Quebec realize the depth of agony and alienation that exists for far too many people in that province.
I am frankly shocked and surprised that the Prime Minister of this country, whose home is in that province, should so often give the impression that his first answer for some of these underlying causes of social discontent and violence is to face them only from the standpoint of repressive and restrictive laws. This seems to me to be almost a council of despair in which we are going to settle for a kind of heavy handed response to the most glaring facets of discontent in a part of this country rather than to root out those elements that give rise to alienation, to agony and to violence. If this government is not willing to engage itself in that area then, surely, it does not deserve to govern and to deal responsibly with the situation.

May 19, 1971
National Security Measures
Secondly, in looking at the question of violence we must be prepared to ask this question: how can violence be prevented? It can be prevented, as I suggested, by going to the root of the long term and general ailments afflicting us, because those ailments alienate parts of society from communities in which they exist. The government itself said that shortly after the kidnappings there seemed to be a deterioration in the will of the people. Have we ever tried to ask why there was this deterioration in the will of the people?
First of all, is it true that there was this deterioration; and, if it is true, what caused it? Was their commitment to democratic institutions so slight and fragile as to collapse at the slightest pressure? I will say more later on about the fragility of our democracy. Why was there such a ready loss of will, if there was such a loss? We ought to attempt to deal with that serious question because, although the War Measures Act was proclaimed and although the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act was enacted, we have not solved the problem. I do not think that any member of the House, including the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice will suggest that we have solved it.
Speaking on the specific question of how violence can be prevented, I find it passing strange that a minister of this government such as the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) who has put some of his thoughts on record in his book, should be so little concerned to justify what was done last fall. Although he has been here almost six years, he has had little to say about a problem that has existed in Quebec for the better part of the last decade. Indeed, in his book the Secretary of State suggested that the government had to invoke the War Measures Act at that particular time because it knew that if it did not respond to that threat there would be another, and another after that. Surely, the government was not surprised at events? It had known about the existence of certain organized violence for the last seven or eight years. As we have heard again and again in this House, there was literally no response on the part of the government.
Speaking on the question of the roots of violence, may I say that if the government was concerned because there were basic gaps in the law, it ought to have said specifically what kind of legislation would be enacted to fill those gaps. It was humbug for the Prime Minister to suggest the other night that the government did not want in any way to predetermine what the committee would do. If this is the government's new modus operandi, one can assume that there will be general references to other bodies whenever it is necessary to do something important. The government will not attempt to bring legislation before the House without referring it first to a committee for study and consideration. It will say, "There is a problem in such and such an area." It might say, to be more specific, "There is a problem in foreign affairs on a certain question, or there is a problem regarding regional development in a certain area. Tell us what to do. Recommend some laws that we can enact in future."

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: That would be foolish, would it not?

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: It would be.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
The government is being equally foolish now by saying, on the one hand, that it will not predetermine what the committee will do and, on the other hand, by admitting that there are certain gaps in the law which need to be filled. When we want to know what laws will be introduced to fill the gaps, we are told that we must wait to find out.
The second main issue that occurs to me, and that is of basic importance with respect to events of last fall is this: Deliberate confusion was created and there was a blurring of some important aspects of the events that took place. If one thing disturbed me more than anything else last fall, it was the fact the government deliberately confused the distinction between political ideas and criminal activity. That was not done inadvertently by one minister on one occasion, but was done on a number of occasions by various ministers. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) made the point that the kind of sweeping action taken by the government would certainly deal a death blow to separatism. The implication was that there was strong support for the invoking of the War Measures Act because some people wanted to get rid, by that means, of this difficult question of separatism. It was thought that that kind of strong action on the part of the government would really show the country how serious we were about that situation.
By deliberately blurring the issue and confusing people, by implying that we would give the separatists a rough time through the kind of heavy handed response that was made, the government showed a kind of intolerance that is a long, long way from anything that we have known in this country. Furthermore, that kind of intolerance is not in the traditions of this country. One of the things that makes Canada unique in my estimation is that despite problems we have encountered during the 100 years of our history, we have been able to sit down and discuss these problems fact to face. Sometimes the discussions have been long and difficult and sometimes the results have not been totally satisfactory. Nevertheless, we have always felt a great measure of respect for each other and for our differences.
Last fall the government showed the kind of intolerance that suggested that when people espouse certain political ideas, the government will not hesitate to utilize its own form of reaction and repression. There might, therefore, even be a kind of state induced violence. Through its overwhelming actions last fall, the government told the separatists what it is prepared to do and how it is prepared to respond to one political front.
I wonder if our fellow Canadians have thought about the implications of that for other parts of the country. What if the people of western Canada should espouse some form of western separatism, as has been suggested on more than one occasion?

speechtext:
Say the three Maritime provinces decide they want to form a union? Would the government, by intimation, suggest that it might use some form of unilateral and repressive action in that situation? Perhaps it would wait until one or two individuals from that area who are not in the mainstream, perhaps, were willing to resort to criminal activity or terror. Would the government then respond and justify its actions on the ground that it is dealing with these specific events while, at the same time, dealing with the over-all problem of political differences? That is not in our tradition, Mr. Speaker. Quite obviously, if that should become part of our tradition, that tradition will be a most dangerous and degrading one. Are we to move away from our traditional posture of public tolerance to one of intolerance? In the field of the espousing of various political ideas, are we to move from tolerance to repression? Will we lose in some measure our right to dissent?
Not too long after the events of last October, the Prime Minister suggested in a television interview that one of the positive things that had happened was that he had polarized the situation. That is polarization all right, but not the kind of polarization one can associate with a democratic country. For all of this, surely there is the question of the government's own perception of social unrest, apprehended insurrections, crises, or call them what you will, and its responsibility to these people. At what point does the government decide it has the right to unilaterally suspend and suppress traditional freedoms, rights and judicial procedures? It has not been clearly defined at what point this must occur. To date, the government has been noticeably reluctant to openly engage in a discussion on that basic question.
There is a third main area that certainly must be examined by any committee that is to do its job responsibly. That is the question of the relationship between civil liberties and public order. Last Thursday, the Minister of Justice referred to this when he was speaking in the debate, because he wanted to point out the problems which seem to exist from time to time in a modern democratic state. When talking about the gaps in the law, he said:

By its actions, the government has indicated that it may not be trusted to protect the regularly accepted procedures and systems of democracy.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this amendment and the main motion, until the last series of interjections by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and other members, my first observation is to the effect that the Minister of Justice was adopting a rather remarkably low profile in this very important debate. His introductory remarks certainly were very short, and I believe rather vague. I was somewhat surprised by that, and I shall deal with some of the things he said as I go through my remarks. I think perhaps the minister's remarks of last Thursday could be summarized in this way. I believe he said in essence, first, that we need some special powers beyond those of the present Criminal Code to deal with the new and growing phenomenon known as the urban guerilla. He insists, secondly, with a bow to civil libertarians, that the government moved reluctantly last October to invoke the massive powers in the War Measures Act to deal with what has been since sardonically described as the most poorly equipped insurrection we have ever apprehended. Finally, in his remarks the minister said that we must do everything in our power to "strike a proper balance between those sometimes competing and conflicting goals of an orderly society on the one hand and of individual liberty on the other".
But in seeking the balance, the Minister of Justice told the House that there are gaps in the criminal laws of the country in respect of facilitating effective law enforcement at times of serious crises. I have said that the minister assumed, up until today, a very low profile. I repeat this because in mentioning these so-called gaps he does not give the country any real idea or examples of what these gaps are. He is singularly reticent on this particular point, except to say that there are gaps. On the basis of these alleged gaps, the government has by resolution proposed the setting up of a committee. I might read the resolution at this point:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to examine, inquire into and report upon the nature and kind of legislation required to deal with emergencies that may arise from time to time in the future by reason of lawlessness or violence in Canadian society and that endanger the existence of government or the maintenance of the peace and public order.
If one reads this carefully, it will be seen that there is no mention whatsoever of two very important considerations. The first is that there is nothing in the terms of reference of the committee with regard to recommending to the government, as a result of its deliberations, whether or not special legislation is required to protect society
5970

May 19, 1971
National Security Measures
from lawlessness. Apparently the minister has already decided this. The minister and the government have decided that special legislation is needed or else he is locked into his particular stance because the whole case for the invocation of the War Measures Act last fall rests entirely on the government's allegations that the Criminal Code was inadequate to deal with the alleged crisis at that time.
The second point-and I feel this is a considerable point-is that there is nothing in the resolution to indicate that the committee is to be instructed to take any special cognizance of individual freedom and personal liberty in bringing forward its ultimate recommendations. On the contrary, the whole thing is negative. It is a law and order resolution. I shall read the pertinent portion again:
. .. legislation required to deal with emergencies that may arise from time to time in the future by reason of lawlessness or violence in Canadian society and that endanger the existence of government or the maintenance of the peace and public order.
So, what we have is a resolution anticipating certain recommendations from a committee before it has even been set up. I would have been much more comfortable with this particular resolution if these two items had been included in it. After all, who could be against studying whether or not we need special legislation? The urban guerilla tactics are a relatively new feature and are not confined entirely to Canada and Quebec. Throughout the world people are fearful of this new phenomenon.
In the minister's opening statement, there is a brief and mild reference to individual liberties, but how can anyone support a resolution which makes no specific reference to the importance of individual rights in a free society at a time of crisis, a crisis the very existence and definition of which is decided by the government. According to the resolution, and by referring to gaps in the Criminal Code, the government has decided that special measures are indeed required. The resolution does not use the words, "such means as may be required". It states flatly that they are needed. As I said earlier, the whole case for the invocation of the War Measures Act rests on the particular assumption that the Criminal Code is inadequate. That is why the minister is reluctant to allow in this resolution a phrase concerning individual liberty. I believe then that it follows the minister knows in his own mind exactly where these gaps exist and has a pretty good idea of the kind of thing he wants to plug these gaps, the kind of legislation he needs to overcome these so-called gaps in the Criminal Code.
I do not think there is any doubt about it, but to date he has not told us, he has not given us any inkling at all. He wants to fob off the whole thing in a joint Senate-Commons committee. He wants to spread the guilt for the resulting recommendations and to evade the direct responsibility for the changes which he has decided upon already. I do not know whether he is gun-shy because of the flak he got from the so-called Turner law. I do not
know what his motivation is, and it is not for me to impute motives, but I sincerely believe that he has a pretty good idea of what he wants included in this legislation, and setting up a parliamentary committee to recommend special measures without allowing it to look into the recent past which motivated the need for them is a mild diversion at best. That is what I think.
I assert that it is incumbent upon the minister to stand up and tell us-he has already responded to a number of other questions-what he has in mind to fill in these gaps, because we have been sucked into similar strategies before. The minister made reference to this in his own little intervention here a moment ago. Before tabling the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act, or the so-called Turner law, each caucus was invited to participate in the legislative drafting by sending suggestions to the government. Our caucus felt that it was a serious search for multi-party legislation to deal with what we did or did not know about a crisis that was occurring at the time. Certainly everyone in the House, including the government, was rather anxious to get rid of the War Measures Act. Our caucus responded to the letter of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and spent considerable time drafting certain suggestions. We have been bludgeoned over the head with those suggestions today, but the point is that we saw the resulting legislation and we saw our suggestions ignored.

Another part of the brief reads:
One way to minimize the use of emergency powers is to force the government that wishes them to sustain the political consequences of invoking the ultimate legal monster, the War Measures Act. For the very reason that it is so politically difficult to invoke it is preferable that a government should have to choose between the enforcement of existing criminal legislation and the invocation of the War Measures Act.
The quotation continues:
Almost nothing in the regular law prevents the police from infiltrating, spying, bribing, and even engaging in electronic eavesdropping. While a valid case might be made that some of these powers could be curtailed, particularly electronic eavesdropping, it is impossible to argue for their expansion. What could be urged-
And I think this is pertinent and appropriate to the city of Montreal
-of course, is the more skillful use of some of these techniques. But improved police techniques don't require additional legislation.
The brief concludes by saying:
In any event, the onus must be on those who seek the enactment of such additional legislation to demonstrate the size of the evil to be purged and the need for the means to be used.
That is what the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) suggests, because you cannot divorce the crisis of last October from this particular committee's concerns or the discussion here today. It is impossible to divorce these two. I believe it is up to the minister to prove to this House that special legislation is needed. So far he has not done that. He has been singularly silent on that. His resolution only implies that it is needed, but he has not proven it is needed.
It is not enough to say that, because most people supported the invocation of the War Measures Act at the height of the crisis its implementation was the right thing to do at the time, any more than it is to say now that if most people are in favour of this sort of half-way legislation, then more is either right or necessary. Isn't that what the committee should be deciding? It certainly appears to me that is what the committee should be deciding.
Sometimes it is very tiresome to listen to lengthy quotations, but I do not wish to be stopped from presenting the thoughts of others just because it might be tiresome. I would like to refer to the writings in the Montreal Star of a gentleman by the name of Dominique Clift, because some of the things that he has had to say about special amendments to the Criminal Code deal with the subject we are discussing.
The implication of course is that urban guerrillas and terrorism are viewed by the government as an almost permanent feature of our society, much like they are in the United States.
Parenthetically, I think that the Americans have never used an instrument as repressive and as massive as the War Measures Act, even though they have dealt with some tragedies, some insurrections of a size certainly magnified by many times the events in Montreal last October.
Mr. Clift continued:
The definition of what constitutes an emergency belongs to the executive and remains a discretionary power of the government. The trouble with this is that information on emergencies is always derived from the police force which is essentially bureaucratic in the sense that its actions, its attitudes and even its methods usually escape public scrutiny . ..
Increasingly, police would be called upon to assess what would be essentially a political situation. The danger is that the cabinet would gradually abdicate its own political authority in favour of the police who already enjoy a monopoly of information on subversive activities. This inevitably leads to increased police activity based on wider surveillance, the accumulation of personal files and the issuing of identity cards.
I am rather fearful of the Solicitor General's (Mr. Goyer) recent suggestion that Members of Parliament should be treated in the same manner as anyone else, when responding to a question on whether or not there was surveillance or a file kept on certain Members of Parliament. Mr. Clift says:
In the realm of law and civil rights the dangers are even greater. The War Measures Act and the Public Order Act have instituted a new type of oifence: the political crime. This is evident by the special provisions which affect the civil rights of persons under suspicion and detention, and which allow for wider and more discretionary use of police powers in times of emergencies. Greater protection should be afforded in such things as access to a lawyer, quick appearance before a judge, preventive detention and compensation when no charges are laid.
He closes by saying:
These are the reasons why the legislation which will succeed the Temporary Public Order Act becomes so important. It may well be necessary to foresee various measures to counter new incidents of terrorism, but as much as possible they should avoid eroding any existing rights. This is all the more important since civil rights are coming under pressure from many other directions, such as credit companies and electronic spying, for instance.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it seems to us the government has not proven its case that the invocation of the War Measures Act was justified in the first place, nor that this proposed resolution adequately protects the rights of the individual because it is biased in favour of law and order. Any special legislation can be used for the purposes for which it is passed, but it also can be used by irresponsible people merely to stamp out dissent, and we are very concerned about that. That is why I will vote in favour of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North. There is still far too much mystery surrounding all the events of last October. My attitude is based not merely on a desire to look back and see whether the government was right or wrong. That is history and people have already made their decision about it. I think the crucial point is that if the events of last fall had not taken place, we would not be dealing with any resolution today that interests itself in the urban guerilla problem.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I shall certainly not call it the Woolliams amendment again. I am relieved to hear that Your Honour does not shock very easily.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North is worthy of support for the reasons I have given and, similarly, a non-amended form of the resolution before us is unacceptable for the reasons I have outlined. I think it is important that we look into the various implications of what we are doing here. A great deal of study has been given to this particular dilemma by Mr. Herbert Marx, in an article which appeared in the McGill Law Review. As far as I know he is no relation of either Harpo or Karl. In this article Professor Marx says:
It is axiomatic that a sovereign state must have effective means at its disposal to deal with emergency situations. Some curtailment of civil liberties is perhaps also inevitable, depending on the gravity of the emergency. However, we must provide checks for unwarranted and excessive government interference with basic liberties. There are at least three such possible checks.
(1)	An entrenched or constitutional Canadian Bill of Rights would offer some guarantees. At least, it would prohibit Parliament or the government from automatically suspending civil liberties during an emergency.
I do not think I need elaborate on that or contrast it with what protection an American citizen has in a similar crisis.
(2)	Parliament can restrict the powers delegated to the government under the War Measures Act or under an analogous law. For example, it should be more clearly delineated under what conditions the government can invoke its emergency powers;-
We have never heard about these conditions, Mr. Speaker, from the government.
-the government should not have the power to deport Canadian citizens; and, it should be specified under what circumstances and with what safeguards the writ of habeas corpus can be suspended.

(3)	Implementation of one or both of the above suggestions would permit our courts to be more vigorous and imaginative in checking abuses of our civil liberties.
There is, however, no panacea for the maintenance of civil liberties during emergency. In the long run, as Harold Laski wrote in 1942, the crucial factor in the preservation of civil liberties "is the existence of a citizen body which is conscious that civil liberties matter, and is willing, if need be, to fight for them."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the debate these last few days on the motion concerning the establishment of a special joint committee to consider legislation required to deal with emergencies arising from disorder and violence, 1 see that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) seems to have been designed to allow that committee or the House to appeal past decisions of the House.
I realize that the amendment seems to be conceived only to permit a revision of the past. And as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) mentioned a moment ago, what we must do now is look at the future. The people have judged the past and I am sure that they are satisfied and interested in the future.
Moreover, those decisions particularly and essentially drawn from that amendment were taken by a large majority vote in the House and were welcomed by the Canadian people and especially by the Quebec citizens, in spite of the statements made by intellectuals and so-called intellectuals.
Allow me to give a personal view and mention that the Quebec citizens are as much if not more competent and qualified, individually or through their elected representatives, to analyse current events while we are living in a quiet period and that the fear of disorder has been averted, at least temporarily. We hope that those conditions will become permanent.
On the other hand, as a result of some speeches delivered in the House, we feel that some members are far from understanding the reactions and thoughts of Quebecers, I do not blame them; I have no right to do so. This ignorance of the Quebec climate can evidently be ascribed to the distance between that province and others and to the misunderstanding and confusion created by various interpretations and slight differences of language for some whose mother tongue is not French.
However, a great many hon. members from other provinces have been trying to get the facts, both by reading objective reports and through discussions with colleagues who have had a very close knowledge of the October crisis. Let no one say that a bill has already been drafted and that this government is merely waiting for the right opportunity to introduce it. It is even suggested that the proposal to create a joint committee is but an indirect way of giving this matter a first-class funeral.
Perhaps these may be the reasons which have incited the hon. member for Calgary-North (Mr. Woolliams) to move his amendment.

May 19, 1971
National Security Measures
If we were to believe certain hon. members who have participated in this debate, we would think, as a commentator put it quite recently, that of his own free will James Cross went into closed retreat for two months and that our good friend the late Pierre Laporte died of a heart attack. Let us be responsible.
The premier of Quebec the hon. Robert Bourassa feels that permanent legislation must be passed. He is supported by his government, his minister of Justice, municipal authorities, the Montreal police, the provincial police force and the majority of Quebecers.
To my mind, it was not necessary to extend the enforcement of the temporary legislation. The inclination of the opposition was obvious and pointed to an endless debate. Moreover it is my humble opinion that the population was then and still is anxious to have a permanent legislation.
It seems that at times members on the other side object to a legislation just because they are opposition members. Some voted for the War Measures Act and even suggested that, as a reprisal, 30 members of the FLQ should be shot for every public figure kidnapped or killed.
Later, their views underwent a change. Other opposition members blamed the government for acting too late and too impulsively or for not having acted quickly enough, since there had been bombints at irregular intervals for over seven years. Does the opposition want to go over the whole thing again? That is what I gather from the hon. member's amendment.
The establishment of this committee will provide hon. members who are concerned with urgent and vitally important problems with an opportunity to hear government representatives, as the Minister of Justice has just said, expressing at the same time his willingness to testify if invited to do so, as well as representatives of police forces and associations created for the protection of civil liberties. And I feel that many of these various associations in Canada will want to appear before this committee.
If we wish to participate objectively in these discussions and to listen to all the views expressed, I am sure that it will be possible to legislate while striking a proper balance between collective security and individual freedom.
I intend however to suggest a formula to the committee to be set up, whether I am a member of it or not. In any event, I want to say that my position is not rigid as I will always be happy to listen to the pros and cons of such a proposal.
Would it not be in order to enact legislation much along the lines of the 1970 act providing temporary emergency powers? However, such legislation enacted by the federal government under its jurisdiction, would be implemented through proclamation by provincial authorities only in exceptionally serious circumstances such as those which led this government to do so last fall.
This law would be recorded in the statutes and could be implemented only under very limited conditions, as I said earlier. In fact, it would be effective only in a passive manner, and it could become operative only in those circumstances I just mentioned.
