subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
The provincial government will make its own decison, being close to the situation.

As a matter of fact, this would be a passive law in the statutes only to be enforced by the government, as I said to the hon. Leader of the Opposition, in serious circumstances such as those that occurred last October.
Had this law been in force in Quebec during the October crisis, the Quebec authorities would have been fully justified in enforcing it by proclamation as the federal government did with the War Measures Act, a gesture that the whole Canadian society applauded.
At the present time, we are inclined to consider only the problems that Quebec has to cope with as a result of the unhappy experience that province has had. However we must not deceive ourselves. Unfortunately, I don't believe I am wrong when I say that other provinces may have similar trouble and that they will be visited with the same virus in the face of pernicious doctrines daily infiltrating all our institutions. I hope I am mistaken in saying that, but such is my opinion.
Anarchists are seeking a vehicle for their theories. They found one in Quebec. They could well establish another elsewhere in Canada or adopt one, making subtle and skillful use of it as they did in Quebec, subsequently stirring up a segment of the population, to achieve the purposes that are well known.
It would then be the responsibility of the province involved to look into the facts and take decision. Provinces have the juridiction, the awareness of facts and are perfectly able to assume that responsibility, just as Quebec did and proved a few months ago.

We have had in the past few months glaring examples showing that certain members from one part of the country do not know about the other parts of the country. It is not by spending a few months in St. Jean, Quebec, and studying French or by travelling as a tourist in Quebec for a few weeks, or in any other province for that matter, that we can really learn to feel the pulse and understand the frustration that subversive elements are continually feeding our people by various devices and subtle methods. I have faith and confidence in the competence and knowledge of my provincial government, as I am certain other hon. members of this House have in their own provincial governments. They are elected by the same process as we are in this House. They are elected by the same people. I have faith in the common sense of the electorate, as manifested in municipal, provincial or federal elections.
I do not feel that the constitutionality of such a proposal is in question. This would be federal legislation, be it an amendment to the Criminal Code or an isolated statute which would be applied by the provinces. This

May 19, 1971

appears to me to be intra vires and not a delegation of powers. We have examples of such legislation. A recent amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada legalized lotteries, provided the provincial governments passed the necessary legislation and issued a licence to a body wishing to operate lotteries. The Riot Act can be read by a mayor or his alternate or substitute or someone in authority to declare that an assembly is unlawful. This is federal legislation applied by the provinces in a given set of circumstances.
I would not want hon. members or the population at large to think that such a proposal would exclude the intervention of the Armed Forces of Canada, if so requested by a province. This subject is correlated very intimately with recent events. This matter falls under an entirely different department. This intervention, however, would have to be and should be borne by the national treasury. The Canadian army, of which we are rightly proud, is the army of all Canadians. Its use, when and where required, should be provided by the Department of National Defence without any provisos whatsoever.
Such a suggestion would not exclude the establishment of a compensation board set up by the provinces in the event of unfair or prejudicial acts performed, perhaps, by over-zealous or inexperienced police authorities. Again, this being a matter of civil law, our provincial jurisdictions would apply. I have no doubt that some agreement could be reached. Would we, in this Parliament, not be over-paternalistic if we did not consider these different points "en bloc", as a package deal?
In the name of peace, order and good government I think that we should, regardless of party affiliations, seek a new definition in this new legislation of organizations deliberately planning to overthrow the established authority by force and violence. Whatever an association may be, whatever name it may use, if it is plotting to overthrow the established authority by extraordinary means, meaning by force and violence-it need not be one that forms part of the FLQ family-then I believe, Mr. Speaker, that adequate instruments must be given to the various police forces to enable them to function effectively under extreme circumstances and to protect the civil liberties we all cherish so much. That is the crux of this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member who just took his seat. He is a learned member of the Quebec bar. Naturally, I was most interested in what he, as a member from Quebec, had to say on this subject. Your Honour will forgive me if I suggest to him that I do not believe the matter can be expressed in the simplistic terms he tried to outline to the House. This is a much more complex matter. It is one of vital concern to all Canadians, regardless of where they live in this country. To suggest that those of us who are not from the province of Quebec have no knowledge of the subject questions our right to make any comments or in any way participate in the debate which deals with a matter of concern, especially to the province of Quebec.
National Security Measures
I wish I could also say that I have the same faith in my provincial government that he has. I suspect there are many in this House who could echo this sentiment. In my province of Newfoundland, there have been many occasions in the past few years to look with concern upon the government of our province because in the name of law and order, peace and good government, the civil rights in our province have been lightly tossed aside on more than one occasion. Perhaps the only way we will ever resolve this dilemma, which faces all of Canada, is to have a bill of rights entrenched in our constitution which will give equal rights to all Canadians regardless of where they live in this country.
We have a federal statute, the Bill of Rights. Unfortunately, it does not fully meet the need because it only covers the areas under federal jurisdiction. Under our constitution, property and civil rights come within the jurisdiction of the province. A bill of rights in this country can only be truly effective if it is ratified by all of the provinces and enshrined in our constitution. Then, and only then, will Canadians be assured of their rights, regardless of what province they are in, and where they may go in this country. As things stand at the present time, it is fair to say that there are 10 different standards of civil rights in this country, depending on the province you happen to be in at a given time.
I would like to say a few words in support of the amendment. I believe that the amendment is important and one which should commend itself to the House. In citing the need for a review of the events of last October in the committee, we are merely stressing that in order to establish whether fair and effective legislation is needed and what type of legislation is needed, we must look upon this task in light of the events that occurred in Quebec last October. We must examine the situation as it unfolded then in order to more properly determine the kind of legislation which is needed. That is what this amendment states. Otherwise, there is the danger that the committee will become nothing more than a useless vehicle, albeit one that is convenient to the government. Perhaps it might even get the government off the horns of this terrible dilemma. In my opinion, it would be utterly meaningless in coming to grips with the problems which generated and contributed to the situation last fall which shook the very foundations of this nation.
I supported the invocation of the War Measures Act, believing that my support was conditional on the government at some time in the future, when it felt it would be in the public interest to do so, to reveal to the House and hence to the public the need for invoking the War Measures Act in the first instance. This is another reason why I commend the amendment to the House. If this amendment is accepted by the House, it will enable Parliament to fulfil its obligation to the people, which it has not done to date. The House would then have the reasons why the government felt it had to take the measures it did to meet the situation last October.
I also supported the public order bill because it was the fulfilment of one of the undertakings of the government that it would replace the War Measures Act by such a bill. This party supported that move because, among

May 19, 1971
National Security Measures
other things, it helped to restore some degree of normalcy to the country at a time, and I do not think this is an exaggeration, when civil rights had been suspended across the country as a consequence of the invocation of the War Measures Act. With concern, I watched this legislation die and wither. I saw and heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) give his explanations in the House as to why the legislation was allowed to go the way it did. We are left with the feeling that we had a hypothetical crisis. We have not been given one concrete fact to back up the government's use of the most severe and repressive legislation this nation has ever had in peacetime, indeed, legislation which was never meant to be used in peacetime. By its very name, I am sure the legislation was only meant to be used when this nation was at war.
To this end, it would be invaluable to have members of the government, officers of the Crown and the Minister of Justice state to the committee their reasons for the action they took. In so doing, they might be able to convince the committee of the need to come up with new legislation. They could contribute to helping the committee determine the type of legislation that is needed. We can learn much if we are told of the events of last fall. Hopefully, if this kind of evidence is produced before the committee, we can produce legislation that will adequately safeguard civil liberties in this country, the civil liberties of those who are presumed innocent. Only in this way can this committee serve a useful function and adequately meet the responsibility with which this Parliament is about to charge it. I find it very difficult to understand why there would be any basic opposition to the amendment setting up the committee.
My basic belief is that the powers of search and detention employed during the October crisis are of prime importance and central to the whole issue. Important as that may be, we must not forget what I consider to be contributing factors to the events leading up to what took place in Quebec, the social conditions, unemployment and economic disparity. However unpardonable these actions were, there is no way that the government can escape the fact that economic conditions in the province of Quebec and other parts of the country last October and, indeed, now, are such as to be a cause of great concern.
By reviewing the crisis legislation of last October, the committee will be in a better position to evaluate incidents and procedures which resulted in the internment of many citizens whose rights were taken away. Most of them were subsequently released without charges having been preferred. I believe the committee should have the right to learn how the list of persons to be detained was arrived at. Were these arrests the result of arbitrary decisions or did the police follow a general blueprint in arresting people at all hours of the day and night? These are questions which are in the minds of many Canadians and they are questions which will be of concern to the committee as it discharges its responsibility to the House and to the country.
Because of the seemingly arbitrary nature of the police action during the October crisis, we as legislators, and
the public at large, are left in the dark as to the reasons for which these actions were taken. These are questions which must be answered before we can usefully set about determining whether or not legislation is necessary to deal with certain situations in the future, and, if so, what type of legislation is necessary.
The facts as they appear at the present time and, indeed, as they have been admitted in the House, indicate that the events of October did not warrant or justify going beyond the powers contained in the present Criminal Code. It is with trepidation that I, as a layman, refer to the Criminal Code, since I am not versed in the criminal law. However, I have made it my business to learn something about the provisions of the Criminal Code as they affect the situation with which the committee will be dealing. Section 46 deals with treason. It covers the use of force for the purpose of violent overthrow of government. It also deals with conspiracy against the state such as to prejudice the safety or defence of Canada. Section 60 deals with sedition. It covers criminal conspiracy and seditious intention. It is specific in dealing with those who advocate the overthrow by violent means of a democratically elected government. Section 64 has to do with unlawful assembly. It is this section which could have been used in the case of public gatherings or meetings conducted by groups, against which action was considered desirable at that time. Furthermore, the effectiveness of those sections of the Code dealing with kidnapping and murder are obvious to anyone who has studied them.
In October, the government expressed the view that the reason for invoking the War Measures Act was the difficulty of obtaining warrants under which people could be arrested in respect of an apprehended crime in circumstances in which, in the view of the government, insurrection was apprehended. Sections 434-436 inclusive deal with the right of police officers to arrest without warrant, on certain grounds, those who in their opinion have committed or are about to commit an indictable offence. Other sections make reference to parties to an offence, persons counselling an offence, persons accessory after the fact, and persons intimidating Parliament or the legislature. These are sections 21, 22, 23 and 51. I should like the minister to tell us in what way sections 46, 51, 60, 64, 434, 435 and 436, dealing with the murder and kidnapping which unhappily took place in Quebec last fall, are inadequate?
It might also be useful to refer to a Quebec statute which gives wide and sweeping powers to the state, powers which are of great concern to many people. I refer to the Quebec Coroners Act which provides for the arrest and detention of persons whose testimony the coroner deems necessary in certain circumstances. The relevant sections of this act are sections 22 and 23. Obviously, the Quebec government had all the power it needed under the terms of this act. In my view, the federal government and the provincial government concerned had all the powers they needed under the Criminal Code.
It is easy to say that hindsight is infinitely better than foresight, but it appears to me that the use of the War

May 19, 1971

Measures Act last fall in relation to the final outcome of that unhappy crisis was neither profitable nor proper. The application of the War Measures Act is a matter for an executive order, and this being so I should like to see provision made for a judicial review of action taken under the regulations so that those who are detained without a charge being laid would have this recourse open to them.
For these and other reasons, the amendment should commend itself to the House. Perhaps the committee might discuss the whole area of civil rights in this country. In so doing it might assist governments of this country, both provincial and federal, as they pursue their task of trying to write a new constitution. Central to such a constitution would be a bill of rights which would ensure that Canadians shall have certain rights enshrined for all time.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we proceed to the formation of the new committee to consider the threat of violence and terror in society, we have the opportunity to run a circus act which could be the biggest show in town, if that is what we desire. The ingredients are here; intrigue, violence and murder. The full range of human emotions can be tapped; fear, hatred and racism. There are many brands of philosophy that are relevant; tyranny, facism, communism and totalitarianism. There could be opportunities for great partisan political gain. Every political party could play. There could be great gains and risks of great losses to all parties and individuals. All of us are on record. We can, each party at this committee, build an election campaign. The promises, the charges and the counter-charges can all be presented to the committee, but I do not think this is the job we were sent here to do. We were not sent to campaign. We were sent to try to solve Canada's problems, not to exploit them, and particularly not to exploit them for political gain. At another and more dangerous level we could emphasize differences in our work, religious differences, differences in development and in values. In this way, we could help to tear Canada apart. I submit that these are temptations to be resisted.
The government has to assume full responsibility for its role in the events which took place in and around Montreal last October. There should be no question or doubt about that. I was glad to hear the Minister of Justice again emphasize the acceptance by the government of its responsibilities. Likewise, the opposition parties will have to assume the responsibility for their positions. The facts and interpretations of the facts have been presented and will be presented in the next election campaign. It will be up to the voters to judge all of us. Beyond that, the issue will be judged by history; who were the heroes and who were the flim-flam men of the FLQ crisis. As I see it, the proposed committee should not beat these bushes. It has a more practical job and one of greater moment to look into.
I followed with interest the case put forward by the opposition spokesmen on the motion and on the amendment. The theme of their remarks was that the committee should uncover what they call the half-truths and
National Security Measures
distortions which were put forward to try to justify the implementation of crisis legislation and to prove that what the government did last fall was shameful. They hope, and they are quite right, that the amendment proposed would steer the committee to focus on an exercise in politics.
Organized violence and terror was not invented by the FLQ. Regretfully, I do not believe the threat of organized violence and terror will end with the end of the FLQ. I, personally, reject the amendment before us because it implies that the answer to the broad question of coping with violence lies in the events of last October in Montreal. I supported the government last October and voted with it. Obviously I, for one, do not concede that the government over-reacted then or that it was engaged in an adventure. To focus on this issue is to defeat the purpose of the committee.
Even if the allegations of the opposition were conceded, the proposed subject of discussion by this committee would still be justifiable and valid on the basis of developments which are visible elsewhere in the world and elsewhere in this country.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: Such as what?

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: Elsewhere in the world there is this threat of active terrorism and violence.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: The hon. member said "elsewhere in this country". I wonder if he would give us some examples?

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: I can give this example. My wife and I were tear-gassed at a public meeting in Toronto about five weeks ago by people who purported to be members of the Edmund Burke Society. We were tear-gassed in a campaign which the police stated had been carefully organized well in advance.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: So, there should have been an emergency declared.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: I am not saying that.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext: What sue you saying?

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
I am making a point and I think it is a valid point. I am glad to have had the opportunity to illustrate it. Violence and terror are with us in this world and, whether we like it or not, they are not limited to the events that took place in Montreal.
Violence and terror have an ancient history, but their evolution in modem society involves something new. There are two new things happening on which I should like to focus. Firstly terror is increasingly becoming recognized as a legitimate political tactic. This legitimacy must be under-cut. In spite of the suggestion which the leader of the NDP made during the last day's debate on this motion, I believe we live in a society in Canada in which the will of the people is expressed in the institutions of government. We have not yet a truly just society. None the less, I believe there are no disadvantaged groups, regions or classes in Canada which have any right or reason to give up hope that the democratic process can work to their benefit. More and more these disadvan-

May 19, 1971
National Security Measures
taged interests are learning to use democratic processes to achieve their ends.
But this is not true in every country of the world. In some other countries the just society is remote or nonexistent. Disadvantaged groups and dissident minorities have no reason to believe that in these other countries their lot will improve within the given order. They have good reason to believe, on the contrary, that the social and political order is determined to exclude them and to defeat them. In these societies, revolution and the use of terror are understandable. They have become legitimate. We are political animals in this chamber and my guess is that some of us, if we were transplanted to some other society and felt the call to improve that society, would be terrorists. In other words, in some circumstances and in some societies, terror approaches legitimacy.
As we in Canada watch the evolution of remote societies in places both far away and near, we see terror and violence on television in our living rooms. For a small minority of us the difference in the Canadian setting is lost. In those countries the leaders of terrorists negotiate with heads of state. They settle treaties and their rights are established. The urban guerilla, the terrorist, the pirate and the kidnapper are gaining new international credibility. This is a credibility these people do not deserve in Canada. This is a new feature of terror and violence, and I believe it requires the considered attention of the committee.
A second factor which lends immediacy to our need for this study is the growing destructive capacity of the individual criminal or criminal group. In the state of technology of 200, 100 or even 50 years ago, throughout the period during which our values of civil liberties were defined and have flourished, there were rather narrow physical limits to the amount of damage and destruction that even the most violent and deranged killer or anarchistic group could do in society.
Along with the positive things technology and affluence have brought us, they have brought on the negative side the vastly increased power of destruction. For example, theoretical studies have been conducted by the Hudson Institute of New York of the ways by which a small group could kill most of the eight million inhabitants of New York City. There are evidently many ways in which this can be done in a matter of days. All of them involve a considerable amount of planning but none of them require very much in the way of resources.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that thirty years ago even Hitler, with the power of a state behind him, took a considerable number of years to kill his first eight million victims. In the last 30 years the evolution in this power to wreak damage to society has been tremendous. I suggest that this new potency of terror must be borne in mind by the committee as another reason for giving careful consideration to the problem. The Minister of Justice has often referred to the delicate balance which exists between civil liberties on the one hand and the safety of the state on the other. I suggest that these new threats to the state have emerged which have not existed before in the history of civil liberties. It is valid, and
indeed it is our responsibility to address ourselves to these dangers.
It should also be observed that the evolution of technology has produced a threat to civil liberties in addition to the threat to social order. We may now exercise the power of the state and of private interests in the state to gather information, to experience, to hear and to preserve. This situation and these powers created by technology demand our concern. Again, this is an area in which attention is required and in which the government is working.
The Committee will require the points of view, the attention and the participation of all the members of the House of all political parties. It is for this reason I particularly regret the decision announced, I hope tentatively, by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) that his party does not intend to participate in the work of the committee. He gave as a reason the suggestion that the government had not given his party sufficient time to make recommendations and that the government did not wait for their recommendations before introducing the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act. I have the record here, and I note it was indicated in the House that as of October 19 all parties had been asked to make suggestions concerning the form the legislation might take. It was not until November 2, almost two weeks later, that the public order act was introduced. Two weeks is not a tremendous period of time, but considering the circumstances it is perhaps unreasonable for the Social Credit party to assert that it should have had more time, bearing in mind as well that it was ample time for the Conservative party and the New Democratic Party to put forward their suggestions.
I suggest it is somewhat unfair for the Social Credit party to boycott the committee on the ground that it was not given sufficient time to make constructive suggestions. Aside from that, the members of the Social Credit party have a special interest in this legislation. It is of interest to them and to their supporters. It is true that their party is a minority party, but there are other concerned minority parties in the House. Certainly, the views of this party should be presented and taken into account by the committee in its consideration of the kind of legislation required in order to deal with violence.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION TO DEAL WITH EMERGENCIES CAUSED BY LAWLESSNESS OR VIOLENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and also to vote against the original motion. I should like to express briefly my reasons for doing so. It seems to me it is quite impossible for the proposed committee to deal with the question of what legislation, if any, is required in the future to deal with the possibility of lawlessness and violence in the Canadian society endangering public order without the most careful review of the October crisis and the action taken in relation to it. The question inevitably arises concerning whether the War Measures Act was properly or improperly invoked and whether the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act adopted by Parliament was or was not necessary. The real question which will face the committee is whether the situation

May 19, 1971

could not have been dealt with adequately by the firm and vigorous exercise by the police, with the assistance of the army, of the powers already conferred on them by the Criminal Code.
How can the committee advise concerning whether or not the War Measures Act requires amendment or partial replacement without determining whether its invocation in peacetime, at the time of the October crisis, was or was not necessary. It is my own firm conclusion that as a matter of fact there was no insurrection or apprehended insurrection which necessarily justified the invocation of the War Measures Act. This conclusion, if it is right, should be a guide to what is needed in the way of future legislation. My view on this matter may well not be accepted by others and the committee will perform a valuable role, if the resolution is passed, in reviewing the facts concerning the invocation of the War Measures Act. The War Measures Act, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) have acknowledged, confers almost absolute powers, sweeping powers, which were not appropriate to the circumstances of October. However, it was used, but it was inappropriate and I believe the committee should determine why it was considered by the government to be appropriate. I think the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice should be asked to give evidence before the committee to explain why they thought it was necessary then.
The vast powers conferred by the War Measures Act included temporary suspension of the constitution and of the constitutional rights of the provinces and of individuals. It enabled the complete abrogation of basic fundamental rights. It is clearly a measure which should be used only in time of clear imminent danger to the whole community. It is perfectly true, of course, that grave and serious events occurred in Quebec last October which required firm and perhaps drastic action, but they clearly did not amount to any insurrection or war. A handful of people amounting, so far as the information I have is concerned, to two cells of four or five members each were involved. This hardly constitutes an insurrection. I placed a question on the order paper asking what was the result of the searches conducted under the War Measures Act and the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act. The reply was that 33 firearms and 21 offensive weapons were seized as of October 23, 1970 including shotguns, rifles, revolvers, other firearms, four bayonets, four machetes, nine hunting knives, one sabre and three smoke grenades. This is hardly evidence of an insurrection. If an insurrection were planned it was the worst planned insurrection anyone could apprehend. It seems to me it would be ridiculous to discuss legislation needed to deal with breaches of public order without examining in detail the most recent and up-to-date incidents, and the measures required to deal with them, in order to determine whether or not such drastic action was needed and to what extent the present Criminal Code would have been adequate.
I am opposed to the motion for at least two reasons. In asking that the committee report on the nature and kind of legislation required to deal with emergencies which may occur in the future, there is the assumption that
National Security Measures
such legislation is necessary. This begs the question. The question with which the committee should deal is whether the present legislation is adequate and whether further legislation, which will evidently be restrictive in nature, is really needed.
There is a respectable body of legal opinion in Canada which the committee should hear. It asserts that the present Criminal Code, with its provisions as to conspiracy, is quite adequate for the purpose of assuring public order. If this is so, the committee should be free to state that it is so, and the issue should not be prejudged by the terms of reference. Additional legislation cannot help but be used, however good its intentions, as an instrument of repression of fundamental rights.
The other reason that I object to the motion is that its emphasis is on one aspect of the matter, namely, the protection of public order. The committee is not asked to determine what is necessary to protect the rights of individuals. As the minister said in opening the debate, these two things should be balanced one against the other, but the motion is not balanced. It is an inquiry into the steps necessary to preserve public order. It does not include an inquiry, which I think it should include, into how, in times of stress and strain, fundamental rights of individuals can be protected. I think that the committee should have the power to look at the War Measures Act and to determine whether its terms are too broad, whether the powers conferred by it are too sweeping, and whether the circumstances under which it can be invoked are too loosely and broadly stated.
Another related matter which the committee should consider is the relationship between the War Measures Act and the proposed constitutional bill of rights which I hope will, before too long, be entrenched in the fundamental law of Canada, namely, the constitution of Canada. The present Canadian Bill of Rights is, in my opinion, inadequate. It provides that any act done under the War Measures Act shall not be deemed to be an abrogation of the provisions of the Bill of Rights. In other words, when the War Measures Act is invoked, as it easily can be invoked at any time, the Bill of Rights goes out the window and is silenced.
The purpose of the committee should clearly be spelled out, and the committee should be instructed to consider, among other things, how the rights of the individual may be maintained even in time of stress and disorder. The committee should have the authority to recommend legislation and indeed, if need be, a constitutional amendment which emphasizes the rights of the individual as well as the rights of the community. The present motion seems to limit the committee in this regard. It is unbalanced and therefore dangerous to the liberties of Canadians, and we cannot support it.
In my view, the most important task of the committee would be to consider the relationship between the War Measures Act and the Bill of Rights, so that the public safety and individual rights may be reconciled as well as possible.
